extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners as secondary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim limitations render a claim directed to a judicial exception patent-eligible (Step 2A/Prong Two and Step 2B of the Alice/Mayo framework), including factors on transformation, well‑understood/routine/conventional activity, meaningful limitations, and mere instructions to apply an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The particularity or generality of the transformation recited in a claim is relevant: more particular transformations (e.g., tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing) are more likely to confine a patent monopoly within definite bounds and thus provide significantly more than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (Gottschalk v. Benson, Corning) show that transformations that are sufficiently definite are favorable. A more particular transformation is likely to provide significantly more. See Tilghman v. Proctor and Diamond v. Diehr for examples of transformative processes that were meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which the recited article is particular
rubrics_metrics.description: A transformation applied to a generically recited article or to any and all articles likely does not provide significantly more than the judicial exception; transformations that apply to specifically identified or particular articles are more likely to provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation that can be specifically identified or that applies only to particular articles is more likely to integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and extent of the transformation (change in state or thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the type or extent of change resulting from the transformation; transformations that change function or use likely provide significantly more, while mere change in location likely does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transforming raw uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded synthetic rubber products (Diehr) provided significantly more; a transformation that only relocates an item typically will not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the article transformed
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformation of a physical or tangible object/substance is more likely to provide significantly more than transformation of an intangible concept (e.g., contractual obligation or mental judgment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical/tangible transformations favor eligibility compared to transformations of intangible concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the extent to which the transformation imposes meaningful limits on execution of claimed method steps; transformations that contribute only nominally (e.g., data gathering, field-of-use) typically do not provide significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo: administering a drug was treated as only a field-of-use limitation and did not provide significantly more. See MPEP §2106.05(g) & (h) for more on insignificant extra-solution activity and field of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity (overall consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: When additional element(s) are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the field, this consideration disfavors eligibility; evaluated only in Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are specific and not routine/conventional, they favor eligibility. If they are merely well-known routine activities recited at a high level, they do not favor eligibility. Examples: DDR Holdings (favored) vs Mayo (not an inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Known-in-the-art can still be unconventional/non-routine
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element known in the art can nonetheless be unconventional or non-routine for purposes of eligibility; novelty/obviousness inquiries are distinct from eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Enfish — features taught in prior art could still be non-conventional improvements to computer functionality and thus favor eligibility even if not novel in the patentability sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual determination required to show well-understood/routine/conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual finding is needed to conclude that an element is well-understood, routine, conventional; examiners may rely on their expertise, specification statements, or court/publication citations rather than a full prior art search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support must be in writing. Appropriate support includes (a) specification or applicant statements showing conventionality, (b) court decisions noting conventionality, (c) publications showing conventionality, or (d) official notice by the examiner. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for how to support such conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of conventional elements may amount to inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements are well-understood and routine, their combination may amount to an inventive concept (i.e., significantly more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diamond v. Diehr, Rapid Litigation Management (repeating freeze/thaw steps), and BASCOM (non-conventional arrangement of generic components) show combinations can render claims eligible. Examiners should consider combinations, not just individual elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine computer function: receiving or transmitting data over a network
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., using the Internet to gather data, using intermediary computers to forward information) has been recognized by courts as a well-understood, routine, conventional computer function when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Symantec, TLI Communications, OIP, buySAFE. Contrast DDR Holdings where interactions with the Internet were specifically manipulated to yield a non-routine result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine computer function: performing repetitive calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing repetitive calculations by a computer has been treated as a generic, conventional use of computers and does not impose meaningful limits when recited at a high level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Flook; Bancorp Services (computer used only for repetitive calculations did not meaningfully limit claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine computer function: electronic recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating, maintaining, or updating electronic records (e.g., shadow accounts, activity logs) is recognized as routine, conventional computer activity when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Alice (shadow accounts); Ultramercial (updating activity log). Such recitations at a high level may not render a claim eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine computer function: storing and retrieving information in memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic claims reciting storing and retrieving information in memory are examples of well-understood, routine computer functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Versata; OIP Technologies. Generic storage/retrieval recitations often do not supply significantly more than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine computer function: electronic scanning/extracting data from documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (e.g., OCR) is recognized as a routine, conventional activity when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Content Extraction and Transmission (OCR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine computer function: web browser navigation functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A web browser’s back and forward button functionality, when recited generically, has been recognized as a routine, conventional computer function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Internet Patent Corp. v. Active Network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: determining biomarker level
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means has been recognized as a well-understood, routine, conventional laboratory technique when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Mayo; Cleveland Clinic Foundation. Such generic measurement steps may not provide significantly more than a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: PCR amplification and detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA is a court-recognized routine laboratory technique when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Genetic Technologies; Ariosa Diagnostics. Generic recitation of PCR may be well-understood/conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: detecting DNA or enzymes
rubrics_metrics.description: Detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample is recognized as well-understood and routine when claimed at a high level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Sequenom; Cleveland Clinic Foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: immunization
rubrics_metrics.description: Immunizing a patient against a disease has been recognized as a routine/conventional activity in some contexts when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Classen Immunotherapies. Note immunization steps in claims can interact with other considerations (e.g., if integrated meaningfully they may favor eligibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: DNA sequencing and amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences, and analyzing DNA to provide sequence information or detect allelic variants, are examples of routine, conventional laboratory activities when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Ambry Genetics; Genetic Technologies; University of Utah Research Foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine life-science technique: freezing and thawing cells
rubrics_metrics.description: Freezing and thawing cells have been recognized by courts as well-understood, routine laboratory activity when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Rapid Litigation Management (but repetition contrary to the art rendered claims inventive in that case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine activities (other fields): recording a customer’s order
rubrics_metrics.description: Recording a customer’s order is an example of an activity courts have found to be routine and conventional when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Apple v. Ameranth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine activities (other fields): shuffling/dealing a deck of cards
rubrics_metrics.description: Shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards can be a routine conventional activity when recited in claims at a high level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine activities (other fields): restricting access by requiring ad viewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a consumer to view an advertisement to access media has been considered a routine, conventional activity when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Ultramercial (requiring viewing an advertisement to access content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine activities (other fields): presenting offers and gathering statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting offers and gathering statistics were treated as routine, conventional activities when recited at a high level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: OIP Technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine activities (other fields): determining an estimated outcome and setting a price
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining an estimated outcome and setting a price are examples of routine activities recognized by courts when claimed generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: OIP Technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized routine activities (other fields): arranging hierarchies, sorting, and pricing determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Arranging a hierarchy of groups, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information and determining the price have been found routine/conventional when recited generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Versata v. SAP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations (overall consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the judicial exception to a particular technological environment; such meaningful limitations can transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter (relevant in Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(d) are meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more or integrate the exception into a practical application. Diehr and Classen are examples of meaningful limitations; Alice is an example where recited elements did not meaningfully limit the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment or prophylaxis limitations as meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment or prophylaxis steps (e.g., immunizing subjects according to an identified schedule) can be meaningful limitations because they integrate an abstract analysis into a specific, tangible method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classen: analysis step plus an immunization step resulted in a practical application (moving from abstract principle to specific application). Such limitations overlap with Step 2A Prong Two particular treatment/prophylaxis consideration (MPEP §2106.04(d)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether additional elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception, examiners must evaluate elements both individually and as a combination; combinations may render the claim eligible even if individual elements do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diamond v. Diehr and BASCOM illustrate that combinations of steps or generic components arranged non-conventionally may be patent-eligible. Examiners should explain on the record why elements meaningfully limit the claim when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (the 'apply it' test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements are no more than a recitation of the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) — i.e., mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception (often on a generic computer); such recitations do not render an abstract idea eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples: Mayo (measuring metabolites was just an instruction to apply), Alice (recitation of computer amounted to mere instructions), Benson (conversion algorithm had no meaningful practical application absent a particular computer implementation). Examiners should avoid treating this as requiring narrow claims; broad claims can be eligible. Overlaps with other considerations (improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood conventional activity) should be evaluated to assist the analysis. Examiners should explain why limitations do not meaningfully limit when making a rejection.
